title: the dice game
hook: before the first throw, Yudhishthira calls the game deceit, Shakuni dares him, and he plays anyway

segments.voice: Yesterday in the dice game, the blind king had a hall built, and sent Vidura, who had warned against it, to carry the invitation. Your line was let a worry change one thing. Did you let someone's worry change one thing before you went ahead? Day seven hundred sixty-seven.

Vidura has delivered the invitation, and Yudhishthira has come. The new hall is ready. The guests are seated, the cloth is spread, and the dice are out. Before anyone throws, there's a conversation, and it's easy to hurry past it on the way to the drama. Don't. Everything that follows is already folded inside it. Yudhishthira says plainly what he thinks of this kind of game. Shakuni answers him, and the answer has a hook in it. And a choice gets made in the open, before the elders have even taken their seats. Today, the talk before the first throw.
screen: `THE BOARD IS SET.` → `A CONVERSATION FIRST.` → `A CHOICE MADE IN THE OPEN.`

segments.voice: In the telling, Shakuni opens. The hall is full, he says; it's time to play. Yudhishthira doesn't pretend. He says that gambling of this kind is deceit, that there's no warrior's courage in it, and he asks Shakuni not to beat them by crooked means. Shakuni has an answer ready, and it's clever. Every contest, he says, is one person knowing more than another. A skilled player beats an unskilled one, a learned person beats one who isn't, and nobody calls that cheating. Then the sting: if you're afraid, don't play. Yudhishthira's reply is the hinge of the whole episode. Called to play, he says, I don't turn back; that's my vow. And he adds that fate rules everyone. So he asks who he'll be playing against. Duryodhana answers: I'll put up the wealth, and my uncle Shakuni will throw for me. Yudhishthira sees the problem at once. One man playing with another's stake, he says, seems to him against the rules. But if that's how they want it, let it begin. Look at what happened in those few lines. He named the danger. He named the unfairness. He was told, nearly in so many words, that refusing would look like fear. And he walked forward anyway, holding a vow and a belief about fate. Some readers call that integrity. Others call it pride. The poem gives both of them something to hold. The elders come in and take their seats, Bhishma, Drona, Kripa and Vidura among them, the poem says with heavy hearts. Yudhishthira puts down his first stake, a costly pearl set in gold. Shakuni throws. And he wins.
screen: `YUDHISHTHIRA: THIS GAME IS DECEIT.` · `SHAKUNI: IF YOU'RE AFRAID, DON'T PLAY.` · `CALLED TO PLAY, I DON'T TURN BACK.` · `ONE MAN THROWS FOR ANOTHER.` · then, large: `THE FIRST STAKE: A PEARL SET IN GOLD.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind a rule you keep for yourself, one you're a little proud of: I always finish what I start, I never say no to family, I don't back down. Say it quietly to yourself. Then ask it one question: has it ever walked you somewhere you'd already said out loud was a mistake? Don't drop the rule, and don't defend it. Just hold it up to the light for a few breaths. If you pray, you can bring that rule into your prayer. If not, simply let the breath carry it. The bell holds the time.
Vrata, a vow that won't let him turn back. Before the first throw, a warning spoken aloud, a dare to answer it, and this vow that walks a king to the board.
Your line: ask whose voice that is. Today, if you hear yourself say I can't back down now, stop and ask whose voice that is. Day seven hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: The dice scene is retold in homes, on stage and on screen, and the talk before the first throw is a place where readers and listeners stop to argue about Yudhishthira's choice.

fork.setup: you're Yudhishthira. Duryodhana says his uncle will throw the dice for him, with Duryodhana's wealth. what do you do?
options: refuse to play against a stand-in.
say it's against the rules, then play anyway.
insist that Duryodhana throw for himself.
fork.reveal: he says one man playing for another seems against the rules, then agrees: if they're set on it, let it begin.

original.note: Sanskrit vrata: a vow or sacred resolve, the kind Yudhishthira says won't let him turn back.

trapdoor: what you thought: Yudhishthira walked into the game blind.
what it means: he named the deceit out loud, then played because his vow wouldn't let him refuse.
what a scholar hears: the scene sets a king's own rule of honor against his own warning, so the fall begins with something he values.
recall: mocked Bhishma with a bird fable

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Dyuta Parva (Shakuni and Yudhishthira before the game; Duryodhana names Shakuni to throw for him; the elders take their seats; the first stake)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli: Yudhishthira calls deceitful gambling sinful and without kshatriya prowess; Shakuni's reply that a skilled player beating an unskilled one is not called deceit, and 'if you are afraid, desist'; Yudhishthira's 'summoned, I do not withdraw' as his vow, with fate all-powerful.
Confirm Yudhishthira's objection that playing through another's agency seems contrary to rule.
Confirm the elders who enter (Bhishma, Drona, Kripa, Vidura) and the phrase about cheerless or heavy hearts.
Confirm the first stake: Ganguli has a costly pearl set in gold.
Original: vrata is offered as the general word for a vow; the script does not claim this word appears in the Sanskrit here. A Keeper may prefer null.
Review picks up day 766 (Vidura sent to carry the invitation). Yudhishthira's journey and arrival are skipped to keep the day on the talk before the first throw.

Editor: hook no longer says the elders were watching the talk (the teach has them enter afterward); first stake changed from 'a string of pearls' to 'a costly pearl set in gold' to follow Ganguli more closely, in voice, screen and match.

Audit: practice rewritten because it repeated day 766's practice (saying yes while part of you says no); new practice works from Yudhishthira's own rule (his vow). Review question reworded (was garbled: 'did a trusted worry change one thing').
